content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Identify the limiting reactant in a reaction
Explain why one reactant limits the amount of product
Calculate the mass of product using the limiting reactant
Identify the excess reactant and calculate how much is left over
In real reactions, we rarely have exactly the right amounts of reactants. Usually, one reactant will run out first - this is the
. Understanding this concept is essential for predicting how much product will form.
is the reactant that is completely used up in a reaction. It limits (determines) the amount of product that can be formed.
is left over at the end of the reaction.
If you have 10 slices of bread and 8 slices of cheese
Each sandwich needs 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese
Bread runs out first → bread is limiting
3 slices of cheese are left over (excess)
Divide each by its coefficient in the equation
The smallest value indicates the limiting reactant
Use the ratio to see which would be completely used up
4 g of magnesium reacts with 10 g of oxygen. Which is the limiting reactant?
Step 1: Calculate moles of each reactant
6.5 g of zinc reacts with 20 cm³ of 2 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the mass of zinc chloride formed.
Step 1: Calculate moles of each reactant
Moles of HCl = c × V = 2 × 0.02 = 0.04 mol
From equation: 1 mol Zn needs 2 mol HCl
0.1 mol Zn would need 0.2 mol HCl
But we only have 0.04 mol HCl
Step 3: Calculate product using limiting reactant
HCl is limiting; 2.72 g of zinc chloride is formed
5.6 g of iron reacts with 3.2 g of sulfur. Calculate the maximum mass of iron(II) sulfide that can form.
We have equal moles of each
Neither is in excess (both are limiting!)
4.0 g of sodium hydroxide reacts with 4.9 g of sulfuric acid. Calculate the mass of excess reactant remaining.
2 mol NaOH reacts with 1 mol H₂SO₄
0.1 mol NaOH would need 0.05 mol H₂SO₄
Neither is in excess - they react completely
10 g of calcium carbonate is added to 50 cm³ of 2 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.
Step 3: Calculate CO₂ from limiting reactant
Assuming the reactant with smaller mass is limiting
Forgetting to use the mole ratio from the equation
Calculating product from the excess reactant

Explain what is meant by the term 'limiting reactant'. (2 marks)
The reactant that is completely used up and determines the amount of product
The reactant that is not completely used up; some remains after the reaction
The ratio of moles of substances in a balanced equation
runs out first and determines maximum product
is left over after the reaction
To find the limiting reactant: calculate moles, then compare using the equation ratio
Method: Find moles → Compare with ratio → Identify limiting → Calculate product
